transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. Um, well, what finally pushed me to come in is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. 

Between patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions... it's just a lot to juggle, and I can't seem to prioritize any of it. I always end up just starting whatever is loudest or right in front of me, instead of focusing on what actually matters.
Have you always had difficulty organizing and prioritizing tasks like this, or is this something that has gotten worse more recently?

Well, it's definitely gotten worse recently. I'd say it's been a real problem for about a year and a month now. 

I got an award, and that kind of pushed me into leading a lot more coordination-heavy work. Before that, I guess I was managing okay, but once I had to start overseeing all these different pieces and other people's schedules, the difficulty with prioritizing just became impossible to ignore.

Before you got this award about a year ago, looking back over your whole life—say, in school or earlier jobs—did you ever struggle with organizing and prioritizing tasks, or was that genuinely not an issue for you?

Well, looking back... yeah, it was definitely there when I was younger, too. Even in grade school. I remember my teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright, but that I daydreamed a lot. And I was always forgetting to turn in assignments, even when I had actually finished them. I'd just lose my homework folders all the time. So, yeah, this kind of thing was happening long before I was even a teenager, it just didn't have the same consequences as it does now.
When you were younger, besides the daydreaming and disorganization you mentioned, did you also struggle with sitting still, or did people describe you as hyperactive or impulsive?

No, not really. I wasn't the kid bouncing off the walls or anything. I didn't get in trouble for talking out of turn or running around the classroom. It was more just... I was quiet, kind of in my own world. I don't think anyone ever called me hyperactive or impulsive.

When you were managing okay before the award—say, five years ago or whenever things felt more under control—were you able to keep up with your responsibilities at work or school even with the daydreaming and disorganization, or were you struggling then too?

I was keeping up, for the most part. I mean, before that award, my work as a software developer was a lot more... individual. I could just put my headphones on and write code. 

I still had the disorganization, you know—my desk was always a mess, and I'd still zone out or lose track of time. But because I only really had to manage my own tasks, I could usually make up for it by just staying a little late or working harder at the last minute. So... I wouldn't say it was effortless, but I was definitely getting the job done. The struggle was always there in the background, it just wasn't affecting my actual performance on paper until I had to start coordinating with everyone else.

You mentioned you weren't hyperactive as a kid, but I want to make sure I have the full picture. Did you ever have trouble waiting your turn, interrupt people, or act without thinking things through—things like blurting things out or making quick decisions you regretted?

No, honestly, none of that really sounds like me. I've never been the type to blurt things out or interrupt people. If anything, I'm usually the one waiting too long to speak up in a meeting and missing my chance entirely. I don't really make rash decisions, either. I tend to overthink things rather than just acting on impulse. So, no, I wouldn't say I've ever struggled with those kinds of things.

You mentioned that you zone out and lose track of time—when that happens, how long do you typically lose track for, and does it happen even when you're doing something you find interesting or important?

When I zone out... it really depends. Sometimes it's just a few minutes, like I'll look at a block of code and suddenly realize I haven't actually read a single line of it. Other times, if I fall down a rabbit hole online or get caught up in my own thoughts, it can be an hour or more before I snap back and realize how much time has passed. 

And yeah, it definitely happens even with things I find interesting. Actually, sometimes it's worse then, because I get so absorbed in one specific detail that I completely lose sight of the bigger picture or the actual task I was supposed to be doing. But even if it's an important project with a deadline, I can still just... drift off. It's not really something I can control based on how much I care about the work.

When you were in school as a child, did teachers or parents ever express concern about your attention span or ability to focus on tasks—not just the daydreaming, but things like difficulty sustaining attention on homework, reading, or instructions?

Yeah, looking back, it was definitely an issue in grade school, too. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but that I daydreamed a lot. It wasn't just the daydreaming, though. I would actually do the homework and then completely forget to turn it in. Or I'd just lose my homework folders entirely. So, yeah, that kind of stuff was happening long before I was even a teenager.

When you were in elementary school, did your daydreaming and difficulty with attention actually cause problems for you—like getting lower grades, needing extra help, or having teachers or parents be concerned about your performance—or was it more just something they noticed without it really affecting how well you did academically?

I don't think it really caused major problems with my grades, at least not back then. I mean, my parents and teachers were definitely frustrated about the lost assignments and the spacing out, but... I was a smart kid, so I usually did well enough on tests to make up for whatever homework I forgot to turn in. 

I never needed extra help or a tutor or anything like that. So, yeah, it was more just something they noticed and complained about on report cards, rather than something that actually tanked my academic performance in elementary school.

Even though your grades were okay, did the daydreaming and lost assignments cause problems in other ways when you were in elementary school—like getting in trouble with parents, needing to redo work, or having to spend a lot of extra time organizing or searching for things?

Not really, no. I mean... I'm sure my parents got annoyed with me when I lost things, but I don't remember getting into serious trouble over it or being grounded all the time. 

And as for redoing work or spending hours trying to organize... I don't really think so. I probably just scrambled at the last minute or just accepted that a worksheet was gone. It's a little hard to remember the exact details from that long ago, but honestly, nothing stands out as being a huge issue outside of just the occasional frustration from my teachers or parents. I mostly just coasted through it.

When you think back to elementary school, did your daydreaming and trouble with lost assignments ever cause you to fall behind your classmates academically, or did teachers ever suggest you might need testing or evaluation for attention problems?

No, I never really fell behind. Like I said, I was able to coast through and test well enough to keep up with everyone else. And nobody ever brought up testing or evaluations. I don't think ADHD or attention issues were really on anyone's radar back then, at least not for a kid who wasn't bouncing off the walls or failing classes. It was just chalked up to me being disorganized or having my head in the clouds.

You mentioned you were quiet and in your own world as a kid. But thinking back to elementary or middle school—did you ever have trouble sitting still during class, fidget a lot with things in your hands, or feel like you had a lot of restless energy that was hard to contain, even if it wasn't obvious to teachers?

No, I didn't really have that issue. I was always pretty content just sitting at my desk. I mean, maybe I'd doodle on a notebook or something, but I never felt that restless energy you're talking about. I didn't have any trouble staying in my seat or anything like that. Like I said, I was mostly just zoned out, not physically fidgety.

Looking back at elementary school, when you lost assignments or spaced out in class—did that ever result in you having to stay after school, get detention, or have your parents meet with teachers because of these issues, or was it really just comments on report cards without any real consequences?

No, there was never any detention or staying after school for it. It really was just comments on report cards, like you said. Teachers would write things like "needs to pay more attention" or "capable of more if he applies himself," but that was about the extent of it. My parents went to the regular parent-teacher conferences, but they were never called in specifically because of my behavior or missing work. There just weren't any real consequences back then.

When you were in elementary school, even though your grades stayed okay, did the daydreaming and lost assignments actually interfere with your ability to keep up day-to-day—like, did you have to put in significantly more effort than other kids to stay organized, or did things just come naturally to you aside from the occasional lost folder?

No, I didn't really put in any extra effort. Honestly, I probably put in less effort than most kids. Things just sort of came naturally to me, academically speaking. So even if I lost a worksheet or completely spaced out while the teacher was talking, I could usually just figure it out on the fly or, you know, ace the test anyway. I never really tried hard to stay organized back then because I just didn't need to in order to get by. It was really just the occasional lost folder, like you said.

You mentioned that things came naturally to you academically and you didn't need to put in extra effort. But I'm curious—when you were in elementary school, did you ever feel like you were working harder than your classmates to keep track of assignments, remember instructions, or stay focused during lessons, even if your grades didn't show it?

No, not really. I mean, like I was saying, I wasn't putting in much effort at all back then. I didn't feel like I was working harder to remember things or stay focused. Honestly, I think I was just kind of oblivious to a lot of it. 

If I missed an instruction or forgot to write down an assignment, I didn't really stress over it or try to overcompensate. I just kind of floated through, so... no, I never felt like I was working harder than the other kids to keep track of things.

Looking back at elementary school, did you ever need any kind of special help, tutoring, or accommodations from teachers to keep up with your classmates—like being allowed to turn in assignments late, getting reminders about things, or anything like that?

No, I never had any of that. I didn't need a tutor or any special accommodations, and I wasn't getting extra time or reminders. Like I mentioned, I was getting by just fine on my own, so the teachers didn't really have any reason to step in and offer that kind of help. I just did the regular work like everyone else.
When you were in elementary school, did you ever repeat a grade, get held back in any subject, or have to go to summer school because of your schoolwork or attention issues?

No, nothing like that. I never repeated a grade or had to go to summer school. Um, since my grades were always fine, there was never really any reason to hold me back. I just passed everything and moved on to the next grade each year with everyone else.

However, critical diagnostic criteria for ADHD are not met: (1) the symptoms did not cause clinically significant functional impairment in childhood—grades remained good, no academic interventions needed, no detention or consequences, minimal parental concern; (2) no hyperactivity or impulsivity symptoms were ever present; (3) the functional impairment is recent (1 year) and situational, emerging only after a change in job demands requiring coordination and prioritization skills.
